mechanism: Ashwagandha root extract has raised T3/T4 and lowered TSH in small controlled trials; added to levothyroxine the combined effect can push thyroid hormone above the target range.
effect: Possible over-replacement: palpitations, anxiety, tremor, sleep disturbance, weight loss, or an unexpectedly low TSH on routine testing.
management: Doctors typically ask the patient not to start or stop either product on their own, recheck TSH/free T4 about 6-8 weeks after any change, and adjust the levothyroxine dose if needed.

sources.title: Gannon JM, Forrest PE, Roy Chengappa KN. Subtle changes in thyroid indices during a placebo-controlled study of an extract of Withania somnifera in persons with bipolar disorder. J Ayurveda Integr Med 2014;5(4):241-245

Sharma AK, Basu I, Singh S. Efficacy and safety of ashwagandha root extract in subclinical hypothyroid patients: a double-blind, randomized placebo-controlled trial. J Altern Complement Med 2018;24(3):243-248
MSKCC About Herbs: Ashwagandha

patient_summary_en: Ashwagandha can nudge thyroid hormone levels up. Taken with a thyroid tablet, the total effect may become too strong, which can show up as a racing heart, anxiety or an abnormal TSH report. The evidence comes from small trials and case reports (grade B).
patient_summary_hi: अश्वगंधा थायरॉइड हार्मोन के स्तर को थोड़ा बढ़ा सकती है। थायरॉइड की गोली के साथ लेने पर कुल असर ज़्यादा हो सकता है, जो धड़कन तेज़ होना, घबराहट या TSH रिपोर्ट में बदलाव के रूप में दिख सकता है। प्रमाण छोटे अध्ययनों और केस रिपोर्ट से हैं (ग्रेड B)।
reviewer: TakeSure curation team (pending external pharmacologist review)

mechanism: Ashwagandha has GABA-mimetic, sedative properties in preclinical and small human studies.
effect: Additive drowsiness or slowed reactions when combined with benzodiazepines.
management: Doctors usually advise caution with driving or machinery and ask the patient to report excessive sleepiness.

mechanism: Ashwagandha has sedative and anxiolytic effects; a pharmacodynamic overlap with antidepressants is plausible but not demonstrated in trials.
effect: Possible additive drowsiness; no documented serotonergic toxicity.
management: Doctors usually ask about sleepiness and keep the combination under review; no routine test is needed.

effect: Theoretical reduction in the effect of immunosuppressive therapy; relevant in transplant and autoimmune disease.
management: Transplant and autoimmune teams generally advise avoiding immune-stimulating supplements unless the specialist agrees; drug levels and disease activity are monitored.

effect: Possible additive glucose lowering with antidiabetic medicines.
management: Doctors usually suggest checking blood sugar a little more often for the first few weeks.

effect: Added hepatotoxic burden alongside methotrexate, which needs regular liver tests anyway.
management: Doctors generally keep the routine liver function monitoring that methotrexate already requires and ask patients to report jaundice, dark urine or itching.

effect: Risk of reduced immunosuppression (rejection or disease flare) and of liver injury in susceptible people.
management: Transplant and autoimmune specialists generally advise against giloy; where it has been taken, they check drug levels, liver tests and disease activity.

patient_summary_en: Giloy stimulates the immune system, which works against medicines meant to calm it. In transplant or autoimmune patients this could reduce protection, and a 2021 Indian case series linked giloy to liver injury in some people. Evidence grade B.
patient_summary_hi: गिलोय रोग-प्रतिरोधक तंत्र को सक्रिय करती है, जो उन दवाओं के विपरीत है जो उसे शांत रखने के लिए दी जाती हैं। ट्रांसप्लांट या ऑटोइम्यून मरीज़ों में इससे सुरक्षा घट सकती है, और 2021 की एक भारतीय केस-सीरीज़ में गिलोय को कुछ लोगों में लीवर की क्षति से जोड़ा गया। प्रमाण ग्रेड B।
reviewer: TakeSure curation team (pending external pharmacologist review)

mechanism: Hypoglycaemic activity of Tinospora is shown in animal studies and small human reports.
effect: Additive glucose lowering: risk of hypoglycaemia (sweating, shakiness, confusion) with insulin or sulfonylureas.
management: Doctors usually recommend more frequent glucose checks and ask patients never to skip meals; dose review is done by the doctor.

effect: Additive risk of raised liver enzymes.
management: Routine liver tests already scheduled for methotrexate are kept; new jaundice or dark urine is reported promptly.

mechanism: Guggulsterones inhibit platelet aggregation in laboratory studies; added to an anticoagulant this may increase bleeding tendency.
effect: Increased bleeding risk: easy bruising, bleeding gums, prolonged bleeding from cuts, dark stools.
management: Doctors usually ask the patient to report bleeding signs, may check INR more often (warfarin/acenocoumarol), and decide whether to continue the herb.

patient_summary_en: Guggul may make blood clot more slowly. Together with a blood thinner the chance of bleeding (bruises, bleeding gums, dark stools) can rise. The evidence is from laboratory studies and interaction references (grade C), but because blood thinners are high-risk medicines this combination is flagged for a conversation with the doctor first.
patient_summary_hi: गुग्गुल खून के थक्के बनने की गति धीमी कर सकता है। खून पतला करने वाली दवा के साथ रक्तस्राव (नील पड़ना, मसूड़ों से खून, काला मल) की संभावना बढ़ सकती है। प्रमाण प्रयोगशाला अध्ययनों से हैं (ग्रेड C), लेकिन खून पतला करने वाली दवाएँ उच्च-जोखिम वाली होने के कारण यह संयोजन पहले डॉक्टर से बात करने के लिए चिह्नित किया गया है।
reviewer: TakeSure curation team (pending external pharmacologist review)

mechanism: Additive antiplatelet effect (guggulsterones plus aspirin/clopidogrel).
effect: Increased bleeding tendency, especially gastrointestinal.
management: Doctors generally review the need for the herb and ask about bleeding signs; no routine test for antiplatelets.

effect: Lower propranolol levels; blood pressure or heart-rate control may be less effective.
management: Doctors usually check blood pressure/heart rate response and prefer separating doses or reviewing the combination.

effect: Raised INR and bleeding risk with concentrated curcumin supplements (dietary turmeric is not implicated).
management: Doctors usually distinguish food use (fine) from capsules, may check INR more often, and ask about bleeding signs.

patient_summary_en: Turmeric in food is fine. Concentrated curcumin capsules, however, can make blood thinners work harder, raising the chance of bleeding; a published case report describes this. Evidence grade B.

effect: Bleeding tendency with aspirin or clopidogrel at supplement doses.
management: Doctors advise reporting bruising or bleeding; food-level turmeric needs no change.

patient_summary_en: Mulethi (licorice) makes the body hold salt and lose potassium, which pushes blood pressure up. That works against blood pressure tablets. This effect is well documented in human studies (grade A).
patient_summary_hi: मुलेठी शरीर में नमक रोकती है और पोटैशियम घटाती है, जिससे रक्तचाप बढ़ता है। यह रक्तचाप की गोलियों के विपरीत काम करता है। यह असर मानव अध्ययनों में अच्छी तरह दर्ज है (ग्रेड A)।
reviewer: TakeSure curation team (pending external pharmacologist review)

mechanism: Both licorice and loop/thiazide diuretics lower potassium; the combination has caused severe hypokalaemia.
effect: Muscle weakness, cramps, palpitations, dangerous heart-rhythm disturbance from low potassium.
management: Doctors generally advise avoiding regular licorice with diuretics and check serum potassium if it has been taken.

sources.title: WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants, Volume 1 (Radix Glycyrrhizae, Rhizoma Curcumae Longae)

effect: Digoxin toxicity (nausea, visual disturbance, arrhythmia) at otherwise normal doses.
management: Doctors generally advise against licorice with digoxin and check potassium and digoxin level if it has been used.

mechanism: Thick, sticky avaleha taken with tablets may delay their absorption slightly.
effect: Minor delay in medicine absorption.
management: Usually taken at a different time from medicines (e.g., with breakfast milk).

mechanism: Herbo-mineral bhasmas can contain lead, mercury or arsenic; surveys of marketed Ayurvedic products found heavy metals in a meaningful proportion. Long-term exposure stresses kidney and liver and can confound monitoring of other therapies.
effect: Heavy-metal toxicity (anaemia, abdominal pain, neuropathy, kidney/liver dysfunction) that may be mistaken for drug side effects.
management: Doctors generally advise buying only GMP/AYUSH-premium-marked products from licensed manufacturers, avoiding long unsupervised courses, and doing periodic liver and kidney tests when bhasmas are used alongside long-term medicines.

sources.title: Saper RB, et al. Lead, mercury, and arsenic in US- and Indian-manufactured Ayurvedic medicines sold via the Internet. JAMA 2008;300(8):915-923

patient_summary_en: Bhasmas are metal-based preparations. Studies of products sold in the market have found lead, mercury or arsenic in a notable share of them. With any long-term medicine this adds a load on the kidneys and liver, so quality-marked products and periodic tests are usually advised.
patient_summary_hi: भस्म धातु-आधारित तैयारियाँ हैं। बाज़ार में बिकने वाले उत्पादों के अध्ययनों में उल्लेखनीय हिस्से में सीसा, पारा या आर्सेनिक पाया गया है। किसी भी लंबी अवधि की दवा के साथ यह गुर्दे और लीवर पर भार बढ़ाता है, इसलिए गुणवत्ता-चिह्नित उत्पाद और समय-समय पर जाँच की सलाह दी जाती है।

mechanism: Methotrexate requires close liver and kidney monitoring; heavy-metal contaminated bhasmas add hepatic and renal toxicity and can mimic or mask methotrexate toxicity.
effect: Liver or kidney injury that is hard to attribute; interpretation of methotrexate monitoring becomes unreliable.
management: Rheumatology/oncology teams generally advise avoiding bhasmas during methotrexate therapy and check LFT/KFT if they have been taken.
